questions.q: Kunal says: 'Solar power belongs in the primary sector, because sunlight comes straight from nature, just as fish come from a fishery.' Test his claim against the chapter's grouping of economic activities.
questions.a: No. The chapter's sector map places solar power in the secondary sector, together with water supply and electricity production. The secondary sector includes providing utilities like water, electricity and gas, which means producing a usable supply for people, not taking a good straight out of nature. Fishing is primary because the fish themselves are the good drawn from nature; using sunlight only matters because power is produced from it.
s: Verdict: no, solar power is in the secondary sector on the chapter's map
Secondary sector includes providing utilities like electricity, water and gas
Contrast: fishing takes a good directly from nature, solar power produces a supply

questions.q: Riya has four cards taken from the chapter's list of present-day economic activities. Three of them belong to one economic sector. Which card belongs to a different sector?
questions.a: Creating software
o: Creating software
Making furniture
Manufacturing computers
Manufacturing drones

questions.q: (a) On what basis does the chapter say economic activities are grouped into a sector? (b) Using your answer to (a), explain why fishing and forestry share a sector even though one is done in water and the other in forests.
questions.a: (a) Activities that share similar characteristics are grouped together into broader groups called economic sectors. (b) The shared characteristic is not the place of work: in both, people depend directly on nature to produce goods (fish, wood), so both are primary sector activities.
s: Part (a): grouped by shared similar characteristics
Part (b): both depend directly on nature for their goods, so the place does not matter; both primary

questions.q:
A coastal village in Ratnagiri district has 170 families who earn a living. 120 families catch fish at sea. 30 families dry and salt the fresh fish in a small unit, turning it into dried fish for sale. 20 families repair the fishing boats or drive the trucks that carry fish to the market in Mumbai.
(a) Which economic sector do the 30 families belong to, and why?
(b) How many times as many families work in the primary sector as in the tertiary sector?
(c) A long storm stops all fishing for a month. Using the chapter's ideas and the quotation from Kautilya's Arthashastra that opens it, explain what happens to the other two groups and to the village.
questions.a: (a) Secondary sector: they take an output of the primary sector (fresh fish) and transform it into another form (dried fish) for sale. (b) Primary 120, tertiary 20: 120 / 20 = 6 times. (c) The drying unit has no fish to process, since secondary activities depend on primary outputs, and the trucks have nothing to carry to Mumbai while there is little boat work, so all three groups lose work. Kautilya says the lack of economic activity brings material distress, so the village as a whole suffers, not only the fishing families.
s: Part (a): secondary, because fresh fish (a primary output) is transformed into dried fish
Part (b): 120 / 20 = 6 times
Part (c): secondary and tertiary groups lose work because they depend on the catch; the lack of economic activity brings material distress to the whole village

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's map of economic sectors.
1. Trade and logistics is grouped with manufacturing, since both deal with goods.
2. Water supply and electricity production are grouped with construction.
3. Banking and transportation are grouped with communication.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A teacher hands out five cards: mining, communication, forestry, construction and healthcare. When every card is placed under its correct sector, the only sector that receives exactly one card is the ___ sector.
questions.a: secondary

questions.q: A sugar mill in a small town in Maharashtra closes. Its 300 workers lose this month's wages, and traders say fewer new shops and workshops will open in the town in the coming years. Kautilya's line says the absence of fruitful economic activity endangers 'both current prosperity and future growth'. Which pairing of the two harms is correct?
questions.a: Lost wages this month harm current prosperity; fewer new shops later harm future growth
o: Lost wages this month harm current prosperity; fewer new shops later harm future growth
Lost wages this month harm future growth; fewer new shops later harm current prosperity
Both harms are to current prosperity, since both are felt by the town's own people
Both harms are to future growth, since the mill will never reopen in the town again

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Today people earn their livelihoods through far more kinds of economic activity than most people did earlier.
Reason (R): Activities that create monetary value are called economic activities.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Give one way in which manufacturing mobile phones and repairing mobile phones are linked, and explain why the chapter's ideas still place them in different sectors.
questions.a: Link: a technician can repair and service phones only because phones are first manufactured; the repair work depends on the factory's goods. Different sectors: manufacturing turns materials into a product in a factory (secondary), while repairing is a service that supports people who use the goods (tertiary).
s: A correct link: repair depends on phones already manufactured
Manufacturing transforms materials into goods (secondary); repairing is a service (tertiary)

questions.q: A class draws a chain on the board: a farmer grows wheat, a mill makes flour from it, and a truck takes the flour to a shop. Which of the chapter's Big Questions does this chain mainly help the class answer?
questions.a: How are the three sectors interconnected?
o: How are the three sectors interconnected?
How are economic activities classified?
What differentiates activities to be grouped into sectors?
What makes an activity economic rather than non-economic?

questions.q:
Long ago, a blacksmith family in a village dug out iron ore, made tools from it and sold the tools themselves. Today, one company mines the iron ore, a factory makes the tools and a shop sells them.
(a) Through how many economic sectors does the work of making and selling a tool now pass? Name them in order.
(b) Using (a), explain why the chapter says that classifying activities helps us understand 'the links they have with each other'.
questions.a: (a) Three: primary (mining the iron ore, taken directly from nature), then secondary (the factory transforms the ore into tools), then tertiary (the shop sells them, a service). (b) Once the work is split among different groups, each depends on the one before it: the factory needs the mine's ore and the shop needs the factory's tools. Grouping the activities into sectors shows which kind of work depends on which.
s: Part (a): three sectors, primary (mining), secondary (tool factory), tertiary (shop), in that order
Part (b): each stage depends on the one before it, and sorting the work into sectors shows these links

questions.q: Ishaan, in Class 4, writes in his notebook: 'The primary sector is a village, the secondary sector is a factory town and the tertiary sector is a big city.' Write a reply of five points that corrects him, using the chapter. Your reply must explain what a sector really groups, and give at least one example that shows the three sectors in a single place.
questions.a: 1. A sector is not a place: it is a broad group of economic activities that share similar characteristics. 2. Primary activities are those in which people depend directly on nature to produce goods (agriculture, fishing, mining), wherever they happen. 3. Secondary activities transform primary outputs into goods (construction, manufacturing, utilities like water and electricity). 4. Tertiary activities are services that support people in the other two sectors (transport, trade, banking, healthcare). 5. One place can hold all three: in Anand district, farmers milk cows (primary), a factory in Anand makes butter and milk powder (secondary), and the products are transported and sold in shops (tertiary). So sectors are kinds of work, not kinds of place.
s: A sector groups activities by shared characteristics, not by place
Correct meaning of primary with an example
Correct meaning of secondary with an example
Correct meaning of tertiary with an example
One place shown holding all three sectors (for example Anand)

questions.q: A teacher puts fishing, mining and forestry in one box. A student asks what makes these three belong together. Which answer fits the chapter's rule for forming sectors?
questions.a: In each, people depend directly on nature to produce goods
o: In each, people depend directly on nature to produce goods
Each was a common way of earning a living in earlier times only
Each transforms a raw material into a finished product
Each provides a service to people in other activities

questions.q: Interpret why the chapter places healthcare and banking in the same sector, even though one deals with illness and the other with money. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. Both are on the chapter's map under the tertiary sector. 2. Neither takes a good directly from nature (as primary activities do) nor transforms a raw material into a product (as secondary activities do). 3. Both provide services that support people, including those working in the primary and secondary sectors; what they share is this characteristic, not the subject they deal with.
s: Both are tertiary on the chapter's map
Neither draws goods from nature nor transforms raw materials
Both provide supporting services, which is the shared characteristic

questions.q: True or False? 'Electricity production and the work of an electrician who keeps the supply of electricity regular belong to different economic sectors.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter's map places electricity production in the secondary sector (providing utilities), while it lists electricians, who ensure the regular supply of electricity, among those whose services make up the tertiary sector.
s: Verdict: True
Electricity production is secondary; the electrician's work is a tertiary service

questions.q:
A student made this poster of the chapter's sector map, but she swapped some cards between columns.
Primary: Agriculture, Mining, Solar power, Raising livestock, Forestry
Secondary: Construction, Fishing, Water supply, Communication, Electricity production
Tertiary: Healthcare, Trade and logistics, Manufacturing, Banking, Transportation
(a) Which card in the Primary column is misplaced, and where does it belong?
(b) Name the two misplaced cards in the Secondary column and the column each belongs in.
(c) Every column still has five cards. Working backwards, name the two pairs of cards she must have swapped.
(d) Her teacher hands her a new card, 'a textile factory that makes cloth from cotton'. Which column of the corrected poster should it go in, and which card already on the poster is its closest match? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Solar power belongs in the Secondary column. (b) Fishing belongs in Primary; Communication belongs in Tertiary. (c) Solar power was swapped with Fishing (Primary and Secondary), and Communication with Manufacturing (Secondary and Tertiary). (d) Secondary, next to Manufacturing: the factory takes cotton, an output of the primary sector, and transforms it into cloth for sale, which is the work of the secondary sector (the chapter says cotton is used to make clothes and shows a textile factory among its secondary examples). It neither takes a good directly from nature nor only provides a service.
s: Part (a): solar power to Secondary
Part (b): fishing to Primary, communication to Tertiary
Part (c): pairs solar power and fishing, communication and manufacturing
Part (d): Secondary, closest to Manufacturing, because it transforms material into a product

questions.q: A grandfather says that when he was young, most people around him farmed, reared animals, made tools and pots, and wove cloth. His granddaughter now repairs washing machines for a living. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
questions.a: As society progressed, the number of ways to earn a livelihood grew
o: As society progressed, the number of ways to earn a livelihood grew
Farming and weaving have stopped being economic activities in today's India
Repairing machines is in the same sector as weaving cloth
In earlier times people did not earn any monetary value

questions.q: In a village long ago, people worked at five things: growing crops, rearing livestock, making tools from iron bought from traders, shaping pots from clay brought by carts, and weaving cloth from cotton thread. Sanjay says all five are primary activities 'because they are old village jobs'. Name the activities in his list that are not primary, and give the characteristic that decides it.
questions.a: Making tools, shaping pots and weaving cloth are not primary; they are secondary. The deciding characteristic is not how old the job is or where it is done: in primary work people take goods directly from nature (crops, animals), while tools, pots and cloth are made by transforming materials (metal, clay, cotton) into new products.
s: Names tools, pottery and weaving cloth as not primary (secondary)
Characteristic: taking goods directly from nature versus transforming materials into products, not age or place

questions.q:
A sorting game has ten cards: extracting coal, building a road, a pilot flying passengers, cultivating grain on a farm, processing tea leaves, a nurse caring for patients, water supply, collecting wood from a forest, a truck driver carrying flour to shops, and making flour in a mill.
Sort all ten cards into the three sectors and say which sector gets the most cards. Then find the one chain of three cards, one from each sector, in which each card depends on the one before it, and explain both links.
questions.a: Primary (3): extracting coal, cultivating grain, collecting wood. Secondary (4): building a road, processing tea leaves, water supply, making flour in a mill. Tertiary (3): pilot, nurse, truck driver. The secondary sector gets the most cards (4). Chain: cultivating grain (primary) gives the raw material; the mill processes the grain into flour (secondary), which depends on the farm's output; the truck driver carries the flour to shops (tertiary), a service that depends on the mill's product.
s: Primary cards correct (coal, grain, wood)
Secondary cards correct (road, tea, water supply, flour mill)
Tertiary cards correct (pilot, nurse, truck driver)
Secondary has the most, with 4 cards
Chain grain to flour mill to truck driver, with both links explained

questions.q: The chapter lists today's diverse economic activities: manufacturing computers, mobile phones and drones; working in banks, schools and hotels; driving vehicles for transportation; making furniture; tailoring clothes using machines; creating software; and repairing refrigerators and washing machines. Megha claims: 'This list has examples of both the secondary sector and the primary sector.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The secondary sector is there: manufacturing computers, phones and drones and making furniture transform materials into goods. But no item is primary: none of them is a case of people taking goods directly from nature; the others (banks, schools, hotels, transport, software, repairs) are tertiary services. So the list shows the secondary and tertiary sectors, not the primary.
s: Verdict: partly right
Secondary examples identified correctly (manufacturing, furniture)
No primary example, since none takes goods directly from nature; the others are tertiary

questions.q: Lata extracts coal from a mine near Dhanbad. Gopal extracts oil from groundnuts at a mill in Junagadh. Both say they 'extract' something for a living. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Lata's work is primary, but Gopal's is secondary
o: Lata's work is primary, but Gopal's is secondary
Both are primary, since both of them extract
Both are secondary, since both use machines
Lata's work is secondary, but Gopal's is primary

questions.q:
On a tea estate in Assam, some workers pluck tea leaves from the bushes and others process the leaves into tea.
(a) Which of the two jobs is primary, and why?
(b) Using (a), explain which job a frost that damages the bushes would hit first, and why the other job would be hit soon after.
questions.a: (a) Plucking the leaves is primary, because the leaves are taken directly from the plants, a natural source. (b) The plucking is hit first, since the frost damages the natural source itself. Processing leaves to derive tea is secondary: it transforms the primary output, so with fewer leaves plucked it soon has less to process.
s: Part (a): plucking is primary because the leaves come directly from nature
Part (b): plucking is hit first; processing (secondary) follows because it depends on the plucked leaves

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Making cloth from cotton is a primary sector activity.
Reason (R): Cotton is grown on farms, which is an agricultural activity.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
A survey of the 60 working adults in Sonpur village found: 24 grow crops, 6 raise livestock, 5 catch fish in the river, 10 work in a rice mill that turns paddy into rice, 3 build houses, and 12 run shops, drive vehicles or teach.
(a) In which sector are the 10 rice-mill workers, and why?
(b) How many adults work in the primary sector, and what fraction of all 60 adults is this?
(c) Next year, 5 of the crop growers leave farming to work in the rice mill. How many adults will then be in the primary sector and how many in the secondary sector? Explain why the mill's work still depends on the farmers who remain.
questions.a: (a) Secondary: the mill takes paddy, an output of the primary sector, and transforms it into rice for sale. (b) Primary = 24 + 6 + 5 = 35 adults, which is 35/60 = 7/12 of the adults. (c) Primary = 35 - 5 = 30; secondary = 10 + 3 + 5 = 18. The mill can only work on paddy that someone grows, so it still depends on the output of the farmers who remain; secondary activities depend on outputs of the primary sector.
s: Part (a): secondary, because paddy (a primary output) is processed into rice
Part (b): 35 adults, 7/12 of the village's workers
Part (c): primary 30 and secondary 18, and the mill depends on the paddy the remaining farmers grow

questions.q: Look at these six activities: growing vegetables in a greenhouse, making flour in a mill, raising fish in a pond, building a road, extracting coal, and collecting eggs from a poultry farm. The number of them that are primary activities is ___.
Amit claims: 'A vegetable farmer and a coal miner do the same kind of economic activity in the chapter's sense, though one works on the land and the other under it.' Do you agree? Test his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter names cultivating vegetables on farms and extracting coal from mines as primary sector activities. In both, people depend directly on nature to produce goods; the place of work (on the land or under it) does not decide the sector, the shared characteristic does.
s: Verdict: yes, the claim is right
Both are named by the chapter as primary activities
Shared characteristic: directly dependent on nature, whatever the place of work

questions.q: A farmer in Himachal Pradesh grows tomatoes inside a greenhouse covered with plastic sheets. A classmate says this cannot be primary because the farmer built the greenhouse himself. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: It is primary: crops are still grown from nature, as the chapter's greenhouse farming shows
o: It is primary: crops are still grown from nature, as the chapter's greenhouse farming shows
It is secondary: the farmer transforms plastic sheets into a building, which is construction
It is tertiary: the greenhouse provides a service that supports the growing plants
It is secondary: growing crops under a cover counts as manufacturing in a production unit

questions.q: Near Junagadh, Hemant grows groundnuts on his farm and sells them to an oil mill run by Sunita, which extracts oil from them. Compare the two activities and analyse how they are linked, including what would happen to the mill in a year when the groundnut crop is very small.
questions.a: 1. Hemant produces groundnuts; Sunita's mill produces groundnut oil. 2. Hemant depends directly on nature (his land and crop); the mill depends on the output of the primary sector, the groundnuts. 3. Hemant's work is primary (agriculture); extracting oil from groundnuts is named by the chapter as secondary. 4. If the crop is very small, the mill has little raw material to process, so it produces less oil: the secondary activity is held back by the primary one. 5. Only Hemant's farming is directly dependent on nature; the mill depends on nature only through the farmer's output.
s: What each produces: groundnuts and oil
What each depends on: nature for the farm; the farm's output for the mill
Sectors: farming primary, oil extraction secondary
Effect of a small crop: the mill has less to process
Only the farming is directly dependent on nature, with reason

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Collecting eggs from a poultry farm and collecting wood from a forest belong to the same sector.
2. Processing tea leaves to derive tea is a primary activity, because tea comes from a plant.
3. The book's glossary describes the primary sector as the processing of raw materials into products for sale.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False? 'Fish farming is not a primary activity, because the fish are raised by people in ponds instead of being caught in the wild.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter shows fish farming (fishery) among the types of primary sector activity, and names catching fish from fisheries as primary: the fish are still a good obtained directly from nature, even when they are raised in a pond.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: fish farming is shown as primary; fish are still obtained directly from nature

questions.q:
Match each worker in Column A with the primary activity from the chapter's sector map in Column B.
Column A: 1. A worker digging iron ore out of a pit in Odisha  2. A woman collecting eggs every morning at a poultry farm  3. A woman raising fish in a pond in West Bengal  4. A farmer growing tomatoes in a greenhouse
Column B: a. Agriculture  b. Fishing  c. Raising livestock  d. Mining
A poultry farm in Namakkal collects eggs every morning and sends them to a bakery unit that bakes packaged cakes from them and sells the cakes to shops. In which sectors are the two activities?
questions.a: Collecting eggs is primary; baking cakes is secondary
o: Collecting eggs is primary; baking cakes is secondary
Both are primary, since eggs come from hens
Collecting eggs is secondary; baking cakes is tertiary
Both are secondary, since both happen in buildings

questions.q: Write four or five lines describing a working day of a person whose work the chapter would class as primary. The goods she produces must then be used by a secondary activity that the chapter names. Say clearly which part of your description is primary and why.
questions.a: Any correct description, for example: Kamala picks cotton on her farm in Vidarbha from morning till noon and fills sacks; in the evening the cotton is sent to a mill where it is used to make cloth for clothes. Picking cotton is primary because she depends directly on nature (the crop) to produce the good; making clothes from cotton is a secondary activity named in the chapter.
s: A believable primary activity described (taking a good directly from nature)
Its good used by a secondary activity the chapter names (flour, oil, tea, cloth, furniture, paper, steel)
States which part is primary and why

questions.q:
A district in Vidarbha has a cotton farm, a spinning mill that buys the farm's cotton, and a shirt factory that buys the mill's thread.
(a) Which one of the three extracts raw material directly from nature?
(b) Using (a), explain what would happen to the other two if that one stopped working for a season.
questions.a: (a) The cotton farm: growing cotton is a primary activity, taking a raw material directly from nature. (b) The mill would have no cotton to turn into thread, and so the shirt factory would soon have no thread either. Both depend, one directly and one through the mill, on the raw material the primary sector supplies, so both would slow or stop unless they found cotton elsewhere.
s: Part (a): the cotton farm, the primary activity
Part (b): the mill and then the factory run short, because both depend on the farm's raw material

questions.q:
The Mahato family in a village in West Bengal does four kinds of work. They grow rice and vegetables in their fields, raise two buffaloes for milk, raise fish in a pond behind the house, and run a small mill that turns grain into packaged flour, which they sell to shops in the town.
(a) How many of the family's four kinds of work are primary activities?
(b) Name the common primary activity from the chapter's sector map that covers the buffaloes, and the one that covers the fish pond.
(c) The family says the mill is also primary, because the grain it grinds comes from their own fields. Correct them.
(d) In a year when the grain harvest is poor, which of the other three kinds of work is most directly hit as well? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Three: crops, buffaloes and the fish pond. (b) Raising livestock covers the buffaloes; fishing covers the pond, as in the chapter's fish farming (fishery). (c) Grinding grain into flour is a secondary activity: it transforms a primary output into another form. Where the grain came from does not change what the mill does. (d) The mill, because secondary activities depend on the outputs of the primary sector: with little grain there is little to grind. The buffaloes and the pond do not use the grain harvest.
s: Part (a): three
Part (b): raising livestock for the buffaloes, fishing for the pond
Part (c): the mill transforms grain into flour, so it is secondary whatever the grain's source
Part (d): the mill, because it depends on the grain the fields produce

questions.q: Pooja writes 'collecting honey from beehives' under the secondary sector, saying that the beekeeper has to take the honey out of the hive. The chapter calls milking primary because the product is derived directly from a natural source. Applying the same reason, which classification of collecting honey is right?
questions.a: Primary: the honey is obtained directly from a natural source, the bees
o: Primary: the honey is obtained directly from a natural source, the bees
Secondary: the honey is taken out of the hive, so it has been transformed
Tertiary: the beekeeper looks after the bees, which is a kind of service
Secondary: the hives are boxes the beekeeper builds, like a production unit

questions.q: Nisha says, 'The primary sector just means farming.' Correct her using two activities from the chapter's list of the most common primary activities that are not farming, and say what they share with farming.
questions.a: Mining and fishing (also forestry or raising livestock) are primary activities that are not crop farming. Like farming, in each of them people depend directly on nature to produce goods, such as coal and fish.
s: Two non-farming primary activities from the chapter's list
Shared characteristic: directly dependent on nature to produce goods

questions.q: 'The other two sectors begin where the primary sector ends.' A family in Pune buys three things: tomatoes from a vegetable vendor, wheat flour from a shop, and a cotton shirt from a shop. For each good, write the activities from nature to the family in order and name the sector of each. Then say which good passes through no secondary activity at all, and judge whether that weakens the statement.
questions.a: 1. Tomatoes: a farmer grows them (primary), a truck driver carries them to the market and the vendor sells them to the family (tertiary). 2. Flour: a farmer grows wheat (primary), a mill processes it into flour (secondary), and it is carried to and sold in a shop (tertiary). 3. Shirt: cotton is grown on a farm (primary), it is used to make the shirt (secondary), and it is carried to and sold in a shop (tertiary). 4. The tomatoes pass through no secondary activity: the vendor sells the farm produce as it is. 5. This does not weaken the statement. It says the other sectors begin where the primary sector ends, not that every good passes through both: here the tertiary sector begins directly from the primary output, and in the other two the secondary sector begins from it. In all three, nothing happens until the primary sector has produced the good.
s: Tomato chain in order with sectors (primary, then tertiary)
Flour chain in order with sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary)
Shirt chain in order with sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary)
Identifies the tomatoes as passing through no secondary activity
Judgement: the statement still holds, since both other sectors start from the primary output

questions.q: A family in Chhattisgarh earns its living by collecting wood from a forest. Which next step by the same family would be a secondary activity rather than a primary one?
questions.a: Turning the wood into chairs in a workshop
o: Turning the wood into chairs in a workshop
Collecting wood from a second, larger forest
Cutting the wood with a saw instead of an axe
Carrying the wood to the market in a truck

questions.q: A family in Banaskantha raises buffaloes and sells their milk. Their neighbour buys some of that milk and turns it into ghee in a small unit, to sell in jars. Both families work with milk every day. Compare the two activities: give the sector of each, the characteristic that decides it, and one way the second depends on the first.
questions.a: 1. Raising buffaloes for milk is primary: the product, milk, is derived directly from a natural source, the animals. 2. Making ghee is secondary: it takes milk, an output of the primary sector, and converts it from one form into another (the chapter lists ghee among the products milk is processed into). Working with milk does not decide the sector; whether the good comes straight from nature or is transformed does. 3. The ghee unit depends on the first family's milk: without that primary output it has nothing to process.
s: Raising buffaloes: primary, milk comes directly from a natural source
Making ghee: secondary, milk is converted into another form
Dependence: the ghee unit needs the primary output, milk

questions.q: Mining is often done with heavy machines deep underground, yet the chapter calls extracting coal from mines a primary activity. (a) What is the good obtained? (b) Explain why the use of machines does not move this work into the secondary sector.
questions.a: (a) Coal. (b) The sector depends on what the work does, not the tools used: the coal is taken directly from nature, not made by transforming another sector's output, so it stays primary.
s: Part (a): coal
Part (b): the coal is taken directly from nature, not transformed from a primary output, so the tools do not change the sector

questions.q: The chapter's table for 2022 gives the number of vehicles produced in India: passenger vehicles like cars 45 lakh, commercial vehicles like trucks 10.3 lakh, three wheelers 8.6 lakh and two wheelers 2 crore. Tanya claims: 'Two wheelers made up less than half of all the vehicles in this table.' Test her claim with working.
questions.a: No. 2 crore = 200 lakh. Total = 45 + 10.3 + 8.6 + 200 = 263.9 lakh. Half of the total is about 132 lakh, and two wheelers (200 lakh) are far more than that, about 76% of all the vehicles. All the other three types together come to only 63.9 lakh.
s: Verdict: no, the claim is wrong
Converts 2 crore to 200 lakh and finds the total of 263.9 lakh
Shows 200 lakh is more than half (about 76%, or other three only 63.9 lakh)

questions.q: The chapter places its table of automobile production in 2022 under the secondary sector. Which reason, taken from the chapter, explains why making automobiles belongs there?
questions.a: Steel made from iron ore is used in factories to make cars and trucks
o: Steel made from iron ore is used in factories to make cars and trucks
Cars and trucks are used to transport goods from the farms to the markets
Iron ore for the steel is dug directly out of mines in the earth
The figures were collected by a society of automobile manufacturers

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter counts building a road as a secondary activity, even though no factory is involved.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the secondary sector includes the construction of buildings, roads, etc., along with utilities and factory manufacturing; secondary work is not limited to factories.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: construction of buildings and roads is part of the secondary sector, not only factory work

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Building roads is a secondary sector activity.
2. A warehouse that stores finished goods before they go to shops is a secondary activity, because goods are kept in it.
3. A pharmaceutical factory is shown in the chapter as a secondary sector activity.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A small textile unit in Tiruppur buys cotton from farms nearby and turns it into cloth, which trucks then deliver to shops in Chennai. For this case, take it that each kilogram of cotton gives the unit 8 metres of cloth. In one week the unit made 9,600 metres of cloth.
(a) In which sector is the textile unit, and which sector supplies its cotton?
(b) Working backwards, how many kilograms of cotton did the unit use that week?
(c) Is delivering the cloth to shops in Chennai part of the unit's secondary work? Explain.
(d) Next week the nearby farms can supply only 900 kg of cotton. What is the most cloth the unit can make, and what does this show about the secondary sector?
questions.a: (a) The unit is secondary (cotton is used to make cloth); its cotton comes from the primary sector (agriculture). (b) 9,600 / 8 = 1,200 kg. (c) No. Transporting goods to shops is a tertiary activity, a service like the truck driver who takes produce to the market; it supports the secondary work but is not part of it. (d) 900 x 8 = 7,200 metres at most. It shows that secondary activities depend on the outputs of the primary sector: less cotton means less cloth, however many machines the unit has.
s: Part (a): unit secondary, cotton from the primary sector
Part (c): no, delivery is a tertiary service supporting it
Part (d): 7,200 metres; secondary work depends on primary outputs

questions.q:
Two units stand on the same street in Saharanpur. One makes chairs and tables from wood using power saws. The other repairs those power saws when they break down.
(a) Which of the two units is in the secondary sector, and why?
(b) Using (a), explain why the other unit is not secondary, even though it works with machines all day.
questions.a: (a) The furniture unit: it takes wood, an output of the primary sector, and transforms it into chairs and tables, as the chapter says wood is converted into furniture. (b) The repair unit transforms no primary output into a new product; like the mechanics and technicians in the chapter, it provides a repair service that supports the furniture unit, so it is tertiary. Using machines does not decide the sector; transforming primary outputs into goods does.
s: Part (a): the furniture unit, because it transforms wood into furniture
Part (b): the repair unit provides a service, not a new product, so it is tertiary; machines do not decide the sector

questions.q: A district officer lists four units in Agra for a report on the secondary sector. Which one should NOT be on her list?
questions.a: A shop that sells packets of potato chips to families
o: A shop that sells packets of potato chips to families
A unit that turns potatoes from local farms into chips
A team of workers laying a new road to the villages
A plant that supplies piped drinking water to homes

questions.q:
Read Aman's paragraph for a class wall magazine:
'Secondary activities take goods directly from nature. Processing tea leaves to derive tea is primary, because tea grows on bushes. Making cars and trucks is a tertiary activity, because they are used for transport. Building a road is a primary activity, because roads are laid on land. A pharmaceutical factory is tertiary, because medicines serve sick people.'
Find the five errors and correct each one using the chapter.
questions.a: 1. Secondary activities depend on outputs of the primary sector and transform them; it is primary activities that depend directly on nature. 2. Processing tea leaves to derive tea is a secondary activity: the leaves are a primary output and processing transforms them. 3. Making automobiles such as cars and trucks from steel in factories is secondary manufacturing; using vehicles to transport goods is a separate, tertiary activity. 4. Construction of buildings and roads is a secondary activity. 5. A pharmaceutical factory is one of the chapter's examples of secondary activity: it manufactures products in a factory.
s: Correct meaning of secondary activities (transforming primary outputs)
Processing tea leaves is secondary
Making cars and trucks is secondary manufacturing, not tertiary
Building roads is secondary (construction)
A pharmaceutical factory is secondary

questions.q: A district has a coal mine, a pharmaceutical factory, a team building a road, a bank and a furniture production unit. The number of these that belong to the secondary sector is ___.
(a) From which raw material does the chapter say the steel used in automobiles is made? (b) Using (a), trace the journey from the earth to a finished truck and name the sector of each stage.
questions.a: (a) Iron ore. (b) Iron ore is extracted from the earth by mining (primary); steel is made from it and used in a factory to make trucks (secondary).
s: Part (a): iron ore
Part (b): mining the ore is primary; making steel and the truck is secondary

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A factory in Darjeeling that processes freshly plucked tea leaves into packets of tea is in the secondary sector.
Reason (R): The factory transforms a product taken from nature into a new product for sale.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Show that a flour mill, a groundnut oil mill and a textile factory could not keep working if the primary sector stopped, naming what each one needs.
questions.a: The flour mill processes grain from agricultural fields, the oil mill extracts oil from groundnuts, and the textile factory uses cotton to make cloth. Grain, groundnuts and cotton are all goods that people obtain directly from nature, in the primary sector. Since secondary activities depend on the outputs of the primary sector, each unit would have nothing to process.
s: Names the raw material of each unit: grain, groundnuts, cotton
These raw materials come from primary activities
Secondary activities depend on primary outputs, so all three would stop

questions.q:
Each product in Column A is made in a secondary unit. Match it with the primary activity in Column B that supplies the raw material at the very start of its chain.
Column A: 1. A car from a factory in Chennai  2. A wooden table  3. A cotton shirt  4. A packet of dried fish
Column B: a. Agriculture  b. Fishing  c. Forestry  d. Mining

A workshop in Jamshedpur does two kinds of work. It manufactures brake parts from steel sheets and sells them to bus makers, and it repairs buses for transport companies. It has 25 workers: 15 make parts and 10 repair buses. Last year 60 per cent of its income came from making parts and 40 per cent from repairs. For its records, the district lists each unit under one sector only: the sector of the work that brings in more than half its income.
(a) Which of the workshop's two kinds of work is secondary and which is tertiary? Give a reason for each.
(b) The steel sheets are made from steel. Name the primary activity at the very start of that chain.
(c) Under which sector does the district list the workshop this year, and what does the single listing hide?
(d) Next year repairs are expected to bring in 70 per cent of the income. Should the listing change? Decide, using the district's rule.
questions.a: (a) Making brake parts from steel is secondary: it manufactures a product in a production unit. Repairing buses is tertiary: like the mechanics in the chapter who repair vehicles, it is a service. (b) Mining: the chapter says steel is made from iron ore, which is extracted from mines. (c) Secondary, because making parts brings in 60 per cent, more than half. The single listing hides the 10 repair workers and the 40 per cent of income that comes from a tertiary service. (d) Yes. With repairs at 70 per cent, more than half the income comes from the tertiary service, so the district should now list the workshop under the tertiary sector, even though it still makes parts.
s: Part (a): making parts secondary (manufacturing); repairs tertiary (a service)
Part (b): mining of iron ore
Part (c): secondary (60 per cent); hides the repair work and 40 per cent tertiary income
Part (d): yes, the listing changes to tertiary since repairs exceed half the income

questions.q: A fisherman in Kochi sells part of his catch fresh at the harbour. His wife turns the rest into fish pickle in a small unit and sells it in jars. Differentiate the two activities by sector, giving the feature of each sector that decides it.
questions.a: Catching the fish is primary: the fish are a good taken directly from nature. Making fish pickle is secondary: it takes an output of the primary sector, the fish, and transforms it into another product for sale.
s: Catching fish: primary, a good taken directly from nature
Making pickle: secondary, a primary output transformed into a product for sale

questions.q: A company pipes cooking gas to homes in Pune. A student puts it under the tertiary sector, saying that it reaches people's homes like a service. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: Providing utilities like gas is part of the secondary sector
o: Providing utilities like gas is part of the secondary sector
Gas comes from nature, so supplying it is a primary activity
It is tertiary only because the company sends monthly bills
It is in no sector, because it makes no product in a factory

questions.q: Using the chapter's 2022 table (passenger vehicles 45 lakh, commercial vehicles 10.3 lakh, three wheelers 8.6 lakh, two wheelers 2 crore), rank the four types from the most to the fewest units produced, and find the gap between the third and fourth types.
questions.a: Ranking: two wheelers (2 crore = 200 lakh), passenger vehicles (45 lakh), commercial vehicles (10.3 lakh), three wheelers (8.6 lakh). The gap between commercial vehicles and three wheelers is 10.3 - 8.6 = 1.7 lakh.
s: Converts 2 crore to 200 lakh so the types can be compared
Correct order: two wheelers, passenger, commercial, three wheelers
Gap between commercial vehicles and three wheelers: 1.7 lakh

questions.q: A potter in Khurja digs clay from a riverbank, then shapes and bakes it into cups that she sells to shops. Split her work into two activities and give the sector of each, with a reason.
questions.a: Digging the clay is primary: she takes a raw material directly from nature, as in mining. Shaping and baking the clay into cups is secondary: she transforms a primary output into a product for sale.
s: Digging clay: primary, taken directly from nature
Making cups: secondary, the clay is transformed into a product

questions.q: Rohan says, 'The secondary sector is just factories.' Test his statement using these five units in Gujarat: a textile factory in Surat, a team building a bridge over the Narmada, a plant supplying water to Vadodara, a furniture production unit in Rajkot, and a warehouse in Ahmedabad that stores cloth before it is sent to shops. For each unit, say whether it is secondary, then give your verdict on his statement.
questions.a: 1. The textile factory is secondary: cotton is used to make cloth in a factory. 2. The bridge team is secondary: the chapter puts construction of buildings, roads and the like in the secondary sector, though it is not a factory. 3. The water plant is secondary: providing utilities like water is part of the secondary sector, though it is not a factory either. 4. The furniture production unit is secondary: wood is converted into furniture. 5. The warehouse is not secondary: it stores goods before they are sold, a tertiary service. Verdict: Rohan is wrong. The secondary sector is wider than factories, since it includes construction and utilities, and not every building that holds goods is secondary.
s: Textile factory and furniture unit: secondary, transforming primary outputs
Bridge: secondary (construction), not a factory
Water plant: secondary (a utility), not a factory
Warehouse: tertiary, a storage service
Verdict: wrong, secondary includes construction and utilities beyond factories

questions.q: A unit in Chennai buys ready-made engines, wheels and seats and fits them together into cars. A student says it is not a factory, because it makes nothing from raw material. Which glossary meaning from the chapter shows it is a factory?
questions.a: A building where goods are made, or components are put together, to make a final product
o: A building where goods are made, or components are put together, to make a final product
A large building used for storing products before they are sold or sent to shops
The sale of goods in small quantities for use by the end consumer, rather than for resale
A place where a product brought in from producers is collected and stored

questions.q: The chapter says wood from the forest is converted into furniture and paper. Write three sentences about a forest village in which one primary output is turned into these two different products, naming the sector of each activity.
questions.a: Any correct version, for example: Workers from Kanha village collect wood from the forest nearby (primary). Part of the wood goes to a furniture unit in the next town, where it is made into chairs and tables (secondary). The rest goes to a paper mill, where it is made into paper (secondary).
s: Collecting wood shown as the primary activity
Wood made into furniture, named secondary
Wood made into paper, named secondary

questions.q:
The chapter shows a pharmaceutical factory and a furniture production unit among its examples of secondary activities.
(a) What do the two share that puts them in the same sector?
(b) Using (a), decide whether a shop in Lucknow that sells medicines bought from the factory belongs in the same sector.
questions.a: (a) Both process materials into products for sale or use: they manufacture goods in a factory or production unit. (b) No. The shop makes no product; it sells goods made by others, which is a service like the chapter's shops and retail stores, so it is tertiary.
s: Part (a): both manufacture products from materials
Part (b): no, the shop only sells, a tertiary service

questions.q: A newspaper headline reads: 'More jobs in the service sector this year.' Which pair of workers from the chapter would both be counted under this headline?
questions.a: A pilot and a software developer
o: A pilot and a software developer
A pilot and a worker in a car factory
A software developer and a road builder
A nurse and a worker in a coal mine

questions.q:
A survey of the main road of a market town in Telangana counted 40 places that provide services: 12 mobile and internet shops, 8 clinics, 6 banks, 9 transport agencies running trucks and buses, and 5 warehouses.
(a) Under which heading of the chapter's sector map do the 8 clinics come?
(b) What fraction of the 40 places are mobile and internet shops? Give it in its simplest form.
(c) A flour mill opens on the same road. Should the surveyors add it to their list of service places? Give a reason.
(d) The mill owner must borrow money to buy grain at harvest time, and must keep his flour for some weeks before shops buy it. Which two kinds of service place on the road will he use, and why are both tertiary even though his mill is secondary?
questions.a: (a) Healthcare. (b) 12/40 = 3/10. (c) No. Making flour from grain in a mill is a secondary activity: it transforms a primary output into a product. It is not a service, so it does not belong in a list of tertiary places. (d) The banks (to borrow money) and the warehouses (large buildings for storing products before they are sold or sent to shops). Neither transforms anything into a product; both provide services that support the mill's work, and the chapter places banking and warehouses among tertiary activities. Serving a secondary unit does not make a service secondary.
s: Part (a): healthcare
Part (c): no, the mill is secondary (it transforms grain), not a service
Part (d): banks and warehouses; both are supporting services, so tertiary

questions.q: True or False? 'The tertiary sector produces no goods of its own, so it plays only a small role compared with the other two sectors.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Tertiary activities do provide services rather than goods, but the chapter says these services, which we may not even be able to see, still play a very important role: they support the people working in the primary and secondary sectors.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the chapter says these services play a very important role in supporting the other sectors

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A technician who repairs mobile phones and televisions does tertiary sector work.
Reason (R): The technician transforms a raw material from the primary sector into a new mobile phone.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Kiran says: 'The truck driver and the fruit vendor in the chapter both help farm produce reach people, and both of them are secondary sector workers.' Test each half of his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is supported: the truck driver transports grains and vegetables from the farm to a factory or the market, and the vendor sells farm produce to household consumers. The second half is wrong: neither of them transforms the produce into a new product; both provide services that support people in other sectors, so both are tertiary workers.
s: Verdict: partly right
First half supported: both help farm produce reach factories, markets or households
Second half corrected: neither transforms the produce; both provide services, so tertiary

questions.q: A bank branch in a village in Vidarbha lends money to a cotton farmer so that she can buy seeds before the rains. Which description fits the bank's work?
questions.a: Tertiary, a service that supports a primary-sector farmer
o: Tertiary, a service that supports a primary-sector farmer
Primary, since the loan is used to grow cotton on a farm
Secondary, since the money is turned into seeds and a crop
Not an economic activity, since the bank makes no goods

questions.q: Compare and analyse the work of two people: Baldev, a mechanic who repairs tractors, and Seema, a truck driver who takes vegetables from farms to a market in Delhi. For each, state the sector, say which sector's people the work supports and how, and then explain what the two together show about the chapter's idea of tertiary activities.
questions.a: 1. Baldev: tertiary; he repairs vehicles such as tractors, a service, and produces no new good. 2. His work supports farmers (primary), whose tractors keep running. 3. Seema: tertiary; transporting produce is a service, as in the chapter's example of the truck driver. 4. Her work supports the farmers (primary), whose vegetables reach buyers, and the people who sell or use them. 5. Together they show that tertiary activities provide support to people involved in primary and secondary activities: services we may not notice but which play an important role.
s: Baldev's work: tertiary, a repair service
Whom Baldev supports: farmers in the primary sector
Seema's work: tertiary, a transport service
Whom Seema supports: farmers and buyers of produce
Conclusion: tertiary activities support the people of the other sectors

questions.q: A packet of tea reaches a family through four activities: leaves are plucked on an estate, processed into tea in a factory, stored in a warehouse, and sold by a shopkeeper. Of these four activities, the number that are tertiary is ___.

A nurse at a hospital in Kota treats a factory worker who has hurt his hand, and he returns to work a week later.
(a) In which sector is the nurse's work, and why?
(b) Using (a), explain how her service also supports the factory's production, though she never enters the factory.
questions.a: (a) Tertiary: nurses provide their services to those who need them, as in healthcare; she produces no good. (b) Her care lets the worker get back to his job, so the factory's work (secondary) goes on. Tertiary activities support the people involved in primary and secondary activities, here a worker of the secondary sector.
s: Part (a): tertiary, a healthcare service
Part (b): the worker returns, so secondary production continues; tertiary work supports people in other sectors

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A teacher and a mechanic belong to the same sector, even though one teaches and the other repairs.
2. The chapter lists communication services through mobile and internet as a tertiary activity.
3. A warehouse, which stores products before they are sold or sent to shops, provides a tertiary service.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: In Surat, four people earn a living around a textile factory. Whose work is a tertiary service supporting a secondary activity?
questions.a: A bank clerk who gives the factory a loan to buy new looms
o: A bank clerk who gives the factory a loan to buy new looms
A weaver who makes cloth on the looms inside the factory
A farmer who grows the cotton that the factory buys
A vendor who sells vegetables from her own farm to households

questions.q: During a three-day strike in a town, three services stop: the banks, the mobile and internet network, and the electricians' repair work. For each, say which kind of work in the town is held up and how; then explain what this shows about the chapter's phrase 'services that we may not be able to see but which still play a very important role'.
questions.a: Any reasonable effects, for example: 1. Banks: a farmer cannot take a loan to buy seeds, and a factory cannot get money to pay for raw material, so work in both sectors waits. 2. Mobile and internet: shops and factories cannot take orders or tell buyers when goods are ready, so goods are not sold. 3. Electricians: a factory whose wiring fails stays shut, and a farm's tube well cannot pump water. These services make no goods and are rarely noticed, yet when they stop, the work of the primary and secondary sectors is held up, which is why they play a very important role.
s: Banks: effect on farmers or factories
Mobile and internet: effect on orders or sale
Electricians' work: effect, and the link to 'unseen but very important' services

questions.q:
Salim is an electrician in Ludhiana. His diary for one week reads:
'Monday: fixed the wiring at a flour mill so that its machines could run again.
Tuesday: brought power back to a tube well that pumps water for a wheat farm.
Wednesday: repaired the lights at a school.'
(a) In which sector is Salim's work?
(b) Which sector did he support on Monday, and which on Tuesday?
(c) On Thursday two calls come at once: the tube well on the wheat farm has failed again, and without water the young crop will dry up in two days; and the flour mill's machines have stopped, but it has enough flour in store to sell for a week. He can reach only one today. Which should he go to first, and how does your choice also protect the other sector?
questions.a: (a) Tertiary. Electricians, who ensure a regular supply of electricity, are among the chapter's examples of tertiary services. (b) Monday: the secondary sector (the flour mill processes grain into flour). Tuesday: the primary sector (the wheat farm). (c) The tube well first. A dried-up crop cannot be brought back, while the mill can go on selling its stored flour for a week and its machines can be fixed the next day. Saving the wheat also protects the mill: secondary activities depend on primary outputs, so a lost crop would later mean less grain for the mill to process.
s: Part (a): tertiary
Part (b): Monday secondary, Tuesday primary
Part (c): the tube well first, since the crop loss is lasting and the mill has a week's stock; saving the crop also secures the mill's grain

questions.q:
A cold-storage warehouse in Agra keeps sacks of potatoes for three months before they are sent to shops.
(a) Do the potatoes leave the warehouse as a different product from the one that came in? Explain.
(b) Using (a), explain why the warehouse's work counts as tertiary and not secondary.
questions.a: (a) No. The same potatoes come out; they are only stored, not processed into another form. (b) Secondary activities transform primary outputs into new products. The warehouse transforms nothing: it stores products before they are sold, a service that helps goods reach shops and buyers, so it is tertiary.
s: Part (a): no, the potatoes are stored, not transformed
Part (b): no transformation; storage is a supporting service, so tertiary

questions.q:
Match each service in Column A with its heading under the tertiary sector on the chapter's sector map in Column B.
Column A: 1. A nurse looking after patients in a hospital  2. A firm moving goods through warehouses and trucks  3. A company providing mobile and internet services  4. A clerk giving a loan to a farmer
Column B: a. Banking  b. Communication  c. Healthcare  d. Trade and logistics

A hill village in Uttarakhand grows apples, and a small unit in the village makes apple jam. Four services work in the village: a bank branch, a weekly truck to the town market, a warehouse, and a mobile tower. Facts: the truck is the only way to get apples and jam to the market; the warehouse is the only place where apples can be kept until the truck comes; buyers in the town place their orders by phone; this year the farmers and the jam unit have enough savings and need no loan. Because of a budget cut, one service must close for a year. In five points, give the sector of these services and whom they support, and decide which one could close with the least harm.
questions.a: 1. All four are tertiary: they make no goods and provide services that support people in the other sectors. 2. They support both the apple farmers (primary) and the jam unit (secondary). 3. The truck cannot close: without it neither the apples nor the jam can reach the market. 4. The warehouse and the mobile tower cannot close either: apples could not be kept until the truck comes, and buyers could not place orders. 5. The bank branch could close with the least harm this year, because nobody needs a loan; the cost is that farmers and the unit would have no lender if they needed money later.
s: All four services are tertiary, with reason
They support farmers (primary) and the jam unit (secondary)
Truck essential, with reason from the facts
Warehouse and mobile tower essential, with reasons
Decision: the bank branch, with the reason and its cost

questions.q: A pilot says, 'I fly people and goods across India every day, but I make nothing, so my work is not an economic activity at all.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: It is economic: a paid service in the tertiary sector
o: It is economic: a paid service in the tertiary sector
He is right: only work that makes goods is economic
It is secondary, since aircraft are made in factories
It is primary, since flying depends on air and weather

questions.q: A lawyer and a fisherman both earn their living in the same coastal town in Odisha. Explain why the chapter puts them in different sectors, and say which sector's people the lawyer supports when her client is a unit that builds fishing boats.
questions.a: The fisherman is primary: he takes fish directly from nature. The lawyer is tertiary: she makes no good and provides a service to those who need it. A boat-building unit manufactures boats, so it is secondary; by advising it, the lawyer supports a unit of the secondary sector.
s: Fisherman primary, lawyer tertiary, with reasons
Boat-building unit is secondary, so the lawyer supports the secondary sector

questions.q: A shop in Patna sells mobile phones and also repairs them in a back room. A student says the shop belongs to two sectors. Decide whether he is right, giving the sector of each activity and the reason the chapter also calls this sector the 'service sector'.
questions.a: He is not right: the shop is in one sector. Selling phones is trade at a shop, a tertiary service. Repairing phones is what the chapter's technicians do, also a tertiary service. Neither takes goods from nature nor makes a new product; both provide services to people, which is why the tertiary sector is also called the service sector.
s: Selling phones: tertiary (trade at a shop)
Repairing phones: tertiary (technicians' service), so one sector
Reason for 'service sector': these activities provide services, not goods

questions.q: Which change in a worker's job would move the worker from the secondary sector to the tertiary sector?
questions.a: A worker in a car factory leaves to repair cars as a mechanic
o: A worker in a car factory leaves to repair cars as a mechanic
A tractor mechanic gives up repairs and starts growing wheat
A cotton farmer leaves the farm to work as a weaver in a textile factory
A vegetable vendor moves her stall to a bigger market

questions.q: A mobile-phone company puts up a tower near a fishing village in Kerala. Now the fishermen can call buyers at the harbour from their boats before they land. Name the sector of the company's work, and explain which sector's people it supports here and how.
questions.a: Tertiary: communication services through mobile and internet are tertiary activities. Here it supports the fishermen, who are in the primary sector, by letting them find buyers and fix a sale before the catch is landed.
s: Tertiary (communication service)
Supports primary-sector fishermen by helping them reach buyers

questions.q: Ananya's cousin says: 'My sister develops software, so she must be in the secondary sector: she makes a product, just as factories do.' Write Ananya's reply in five points, using the chapter, that settles which sector software development belongs to.
questions.a: 1. The chapter names software development among its examples of tertiary sector activities. 2. Secondary activities depend on outputs of the primary sector and transform them into goods; software development does not process grain, cotton, wood or iron ore into a product. 3. Tertiary activities provide support to people involved in primary and secondary activities; software is a service of this kind, like communication through mobile and internet. 4. Software is not taken directly from nature either, so it is not primary; the only sector left is the tertiary, the service sector. 5. Contrast: manufacturing computers or mobile phones in a factory is secondary, but creating the software is tertiary, in the service sector.
s: The chapter names software development as tertiary
It does not transform primary outputs, so it is not secondary
It is a supporting service, like communication services
It is not primary either, so it belongs to the service sector
Contrast with manufacturing computers or phones (secondary)

questions.q: An AMUL plant in Gujarat turns liquid milk into milk powder, and an AMUL lorry then carries the powder to shops in Kolkata. To which sectors do these two activities belong?
questions.a: Making powder is secondary; carrying it is tertiary
o: Making powder is secondary; carrying it is tertiary
Making powder is primary; carrying it is secondary
Both are secondary, since both are done by AMUL
Making powder is tertiary; carrying it is secondary

questions.q:
(a) Before 1946, middlemen bought milk in bulk from the Anand farmers and sold it in the market, charging a fee for this. In which sector was the middlemen's work, and why?
(b) Using (a), explain why forming the cooperative removed the middlemen but not that sector from the journey of the milk.
questions.a: (a) Tertiary: buying from producers and selling to consumers is trade, a service for which they charged a fee; they produced nothing. (b) The milk still had to be collected, carried and sold to reach buyers. The cooperative took care of collection and distribution itself, and AMUL today uses transport and retail stores, which the chapter calls tertiary. So the tertiary work stayed; only the people doing it changed, from middlemen to the farmers' own cooperative.
s: Part (a): tertiary, buying and selling for a fee is a service
Part (b): collection, transport and sale were still needed; the cooperative did this tertiary work itself

questions.q:
A school project chart shows four stages in the journey of a packet of AMUL butter:
Stage P: a farmer near Anand milks her buffaloes.
Stage Q: at a processing plant, the milk is pasteurised and made into butter.
Stage R: the butter is carried by railway to Delhi.
Stage S: a family buys one packet of butter at a retail store.
(a) Which stage is primary, and what reason does the chapter give for calling it primary?
(b) At Stage Q, what does pasteurisation do to the milk, and which sector is Stage Q in?
(c) How many stages are tertiary? Name them.
(d) Floods stop the railway in Stage R for one week. The plant has cold rooms that can keep its butter for two weeks. The manager must choose: keep buying all the farmers' milk and store the butter, or stop buying milk until the trains run. Which choice fits the purpose for which the farmers formed the cooperative, and which sector bears the loss under the other choice?
questions.a: (a) Stage P: the product (milk) is derived directly from a natural source, the buffaloes. (b) Pasteurisation preserves milk by heating it to a specific temperature to kill harmful bacteria; turning milk into butter in a plant is secondary. (c) Two: Stage R (transport) and Stage S (retail); the chapter says transportation, trading and retail are tertiary. (d) Keep buying the milk and store the butter. The farmers formed the cooperative to become independent and control the sale of their own milk; if the plant stopped buying, the farmers (the primary sector) would lose a week's income and be left with milk they could not sell. Storing the butter costs the plant some space and money for a week, but the cold rooms can hold it until the trains run.
s: Part (a): Stage P, because milk comes directly from a natural source

questions.q:
Imagine Ramabhai, a farmer in Anand district in 1942, who milks 10 litres every morning. If he cycles to the next village, he can sell only 6 litres at the village price before noon; the rest turns in the heat. A trader at the edge of his own village will buy all 10 litres at once, but pays only half the village price for each litre. Count money in 'village-price units' (the price of one litre in the village).
(a) How many units does each choice bring him, and which brings more?
(b) Most days he still sells to the trader. Using the chapter's account, give the reason.
(c) In 1946 his village can keep selling to the trader or join the new cooperative, whose dairy collects all 10 litres every day at the village price but asks every member to share the work of collection. Which should the village choose? State what it gains and what it gives up.
questions.a: (a) Cycling: 6 x 1 = 6 units. Trader: 10 x 1/2 = 5 units. Cycling brings 1 unit more. (b) Cycling to nearby villages under scorching heat was a lot of effort for the small amount of money earned, and the milk had to be sold quickly before it spoiled; the trader, a middleman, took it all at once, so Ramabhai accepted the meagre price. (c) Join the cooperative: 10 x 1 = 10 units a day, twice what the trader pays, with no milk spoiling and no middleman. What it gives up is time and effort, since the tasks of collection are shared by every member; the gain is far larger than that cost.
s: Part (a): cycling 6 units, trader 5 units; cycling brings 1 more
Part (b): the effort in the heat and the spoiling milk made him sell to the middleman
Part (c): join; 10 units against 5, no spoilage or middleman, at the cost of sharing the work of collection

questions.q:
A paper mill near Dandeli in Karnataka usually makes 600 tonnes of paper a month from wood pulp. In July, heavy rain stopped the collection of wood in the forests for half the month, so the mill made only 300 tonnes. A press in Hubballi that prints school textbooks on this paper printed 40,000 books in June but only 20,000 in July. A truck company that carries the books to shops across the state ran only half its usual trips.
(a) In which sector did the trouble start, and in which sector is the truck company?
(b) By what fraction did the mill's output fall? Did the press's output fall by the same fraction? Show working.
(c) Explain, using the chapter, why the truck company lost work though none of its trucks broke down and no road was closed.
(d) The mill's owner says, 'Before next monsoon I will keep a month's wood in a large store building.' Which sector's service is he planning to use, and judge whether it would have protected the press's July output.
questions.a: (a) The primary sector (collecting wood from forests); the truck company is tertiary (transport). (b) Mill: 300 out of 600 lost, a fall of 300/600 = 1/2. Press: 20,000 out of 40,000 lost, 20,000/40,000 = 1/2. Yes, the same fraction. (c) A transport service supports the other sectors by carrying what they make; with half as many books printed, there was only half as much to carry, so the tertiary work fell with the primary and secondary work. (d) A warehouse, a tertiary service: storing products before they are used. Yes: with wood in store, the mill could have gone on making paper while collection in the forest stopped, so the press would have had paper for its usual number of books. The primary work would still have been needed, earlier, to fill the store.
s: Part (a): trouble began in the primary sector; truck company tertiary
Part (b): both fell by 1/2
Part (c): fewer books made means less to carry, since transport serves the other sectors
Part (d): a warehouse (tertiary); yes, stored wood would have kept the mill and so the press working

(b) Using (a), explain why recycling paper reduces the need for wood from forests but does not remove the need for the other two sectors.
questions.a: (a) The cart service is tertiary (transport, a service); the mill is secondary (it makes paper, a product). (b) Recycling replaces fresh wood pulp with used paper, so fewer trees need to be cut: the primary work of collecting wood falls. But new paper still has to be made in a mill (secondary), and the used paper still has to be collected and carried, and the new paper sold (tertiary).
s: Part (a): cart service tertiary, mill secondary
Part (b): less wood is needed, but making paper and carrying and selling it still need the secondary and tertiary sectors

At a mill and a press, the wood pulp (wooden fibre) is made into paper and printed into books: secondary, because wood from the forest is converted into paper, a primary output transformed into a product. 3. The books are kept in a warehouse until they are sent out: tertiary, since storing products before they are sold is a service. 4. Trucks carry the books to Lucknow: tertiary, a transport service. 5. A shop sells the book to the student's family: tertiary, a retail service, as at the shops the chapter lists.
s: Collecting wood: primary, with reason
Pulp made into paper and books: secondary, with reason
Storing in a warehouse: tertiary, with reason
Transport to Lucknow: tertiary, with reason
Selling at a shop: tertiary, with reason

questions.q:
A press in Sivakasi must print 12,000 copies of a Class 6 textbook for schools in Chennai. It prints 2,000 copies a day, starting on day 1. Because the trucks that bring wood to the paper mill were held up by a strike, the mill could send paper for only 8,000 copies on day 1; paper for the other 4,000 copies reaches the press at the start of day 4. A truck takes one day to reach Chennai. The schools need at least 8,000 copies in hand by the end of day 6, and all 12,000 by day 10.
(a) In which sector did the hold-up begin, and which sector's work did it slow first?
(b) On which day will the first 8,000 copies be printed?
(c) The press keeps printing whenever it has paper. By the end of which day will all 12,000 copies be printed?
(d) The publisher can send one truck after all the books are printed (cheaper), or two trucks, one after the first 8,000 and one after the rest. Which plan should it choose? Show that it meets both of the schools' needs.
questions.a: (a) The tertiary sector (the transport of wood); it slowed the paper mill, in the secondary sector, first. (b) 8,000 / 2,000 = 4 days, so by the end of day 4. (c) The new paper waits until the press finishes the first 8,000 on day 4; the other 4,000 take 4,000 / 2,000 = 2 more days, so all 12,000 are printed by the end of day 6. (d) Two trucks. One truck would leave on day 7 and reach Chennai on day 7, missing the need for 8,000 copies by day 6. With two trucks, the first leaves on day 5 and arrives that day with 8,000 copies, and the second leaves on day 7 and arrives on day 7, before day 10. The extra truck costs more, but only this plan meets both needs.
s: Part (a): began in the tertiary sector (transport); slowed the secondary mill first
Part (b): day 4
Part (c): day 6
Part (d): two trucks; first batch arrives day 5 (by day 6), the rest day 7 (by day 10)

Under both plans the recycled paper is made into new paper at a mill, a secondary activity. 5. Recommendation: Plan X. Landfill saved: 5 cubic metres under X, 2.5 under Y
The Rs 3,000 pays a tertiary transport service, needed under both plans

Recommends X: double the saving, affordable within Rs 5,000
